clinicalPearls: Caused by usually de novo variants in KCNB1, which encodes the delayed-rectifier voltage-gated potassium channel Kv2.1 that shapes repolarisation and regulates repetitive neuronal firing
Presents as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, though some individuals have neurodevelopmental impairment with few or no seizures
Seizure onset is usually in infancy or early childhood, with multiple types including focal, tonic, absence, myoclonic, and epileptic spasms
The electroencephalogram often shows multifocal or generalised epileptiform discharges and may include hypsarrhythmia
Intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, behavioural problems, and attention difficulties are prominent parts of the phenotype

Many pathogenic variants impair the potassium current or confer altered channel properties, disturbing the balance of excitability rather than acting like classic gain-of-function sodium channelopathies
Broad-spectrum antiseizure agents are generally used, and no single medication is uniformly effective
reference.pathophysiology: KCNB1 encodes Kv2.1, a delayed-rectifier voltage-gated potassium channel that carries a major outward potassium current controlling membrane repolarisation, spike-frequency adaptation, and the ability of neurons to fire repetitively. Kv2.1 also has a structural role in organising membrane microdomains. Pathogenic variants disrupt channel gating, selectivity, or expression, and can additionally alter non-conducting functions; the net effect is impaired regulation of neuronal excitability. This dysfunction lowers the seizure threshold and disturbs developmental network activity, producing the combined epileptic and neurodevelopmental phenotype seen clinically.
additionalDifferentials: KCNQ2 and KCNA2 potassium channel encephalopathies
SCN2A and SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
Other genetic causes of infantile-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the KCNB1 variant
Electroencephalography to characterise multifocal or generalised discharges
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes
Where available, functional characterisation of the variant
redFlags: Evolution to epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia
Drug-resistant mixed seizures with developmental regression
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have intellectual disability with behavioural and autistic features; seizures range from readily controlled to drug-resistant, and cognitive outcome is generally guarded even when seizures improve.
pitfalls: Assuming absent seizures excludes the diagnosis in a child with neurodevelopmental impairment
Applying sodium-channelopathy treatment logic to a potassium channel disorder
Underestimating the behavioural and attention comorbidity
Missing evolving epileptic spasms on the electroencephalogram
references: GeneReviews and OMIM resources on KCNB1-related disorders
ILAE resources on potassium channel developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
management: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medications such as valproate, levetiracetam or benzodiazepines titrated to the seizure types, as no targeted therapy exists
Consideration of the ketogenic diet for drug-resistant seizures
Multidisciplinary developmental support with speech, occupational and physiotherapy for the intellectual disability and autistic features
Behavioural, psychological and educational interventions for attention difficulties and behavioural problems
EEG-guided reassessment of the antiseizure regimen as the multifocal or generalised discharges and seizure types evolve
Rescue benzodiazepine protocol and a status epilepticus plan for prolonged or clustering seizures
Clinical genetics counselling; most variants are de novo so recurrence risk is usually low, but parental testing refines advice
